idiom_name: optional catch binding plus a narrowed or typed catch clause
implementation_notes: TypeScript inherits JavaScript's optional catch binding, so `catch { }` is the language-level mute; TS-specific, the useUnknownInCatchVariables flag (introduced in TypeScript 4.4 and enabled under strict) types a bound catch variable as unknown instead of any, so reading a muted error requires an explicit narrowing first. A mute therefore either omits the binding or documents why the unknown value is not examined. Fire-and-forget promises use the JavaScript form plus the lint-facing `void` operator (`void p.catch(() => {})`), and eslint rules (no-empty, no-unused-vars) need a per-site comment or suppression so the mute reads as intentional.
pitfalls: Under strict settings the catch variable is unknown, so `catch (e) { e.message }` needs narrowing - casting it to any to make the mute compile defeats the very check that documents the risk.

`catch {}` silently widens a typed wrapper's error contract (a function typed to never throw, or whose callers handle a specific error) - document the mute at the boundary or narrow the declared type instead.

An ignored rejection also erases type information (a rejected promise of a generic result); the `void`-marked empty handler is fine for telemetry, but for anything a caller awaits it converts a typed failure into an untyped non-event.
